d: Azor, son of Eliakim and father of Zadok, an ancestor of Jesus.

e.t: Azor is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears twice, in Matthew 1:13 and Matthew 1:14. The English Bible preserves it as “Azor,” so its meaning is chiefly its identity as the person named. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain Azor’s specific role in either passage.

This word describes someone as “blameless” or “innocent”—not guilty of wrongdoing or deserving blame. It presents a person in a morally clean and harmless light. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, so its meaning is clear but its use is relatively limited. One occurrence is rendered “innocent,” while the other is in Hebrews. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

“One another” refers to people in relation to each other, expressing a reciprocal connection or action. It can describe what people do toward each other, how they regard one another, or the relationship shared among them. This word appears 100 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that it commonly describes interaction within a group or between individuals rather than action directed toward only one person.

This word means “innocent.” It describes a person who is not guilty of the matter under consideration. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Matthew 12, so its normal meaning is supported by a small number of uses rather than a broad range of contexts. The surrounding passage determines exactly how the description applies in each verse.

This word means “proconsul,” a title for a governing official. It identifies a person holding public authority rather than describing an action, quality, or religious practice. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, all in Acts, where it serves as an official title. The word appears in Acts 13, Acts 18, and Acts 19, including both singular and plural references. Its basic meaning is therefore a provincial ruler or administrator called a proconsul.

d: (a) to kill, destroy, (b) to lose, to be perishing (the resultant death being viewed as certain).

e.t: This word means “to destroy”: to bring something to an end through destruction. It can describe someone destroying another thing, or something being destroyed, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 90 times, showing that it is used in many settings rather than having only one narrow application. Its central idea remains destruction. The surrounding words determine what is destroyed and how the action is expressed in a particular verse.

d: To withdraw from, take leave of, renounce, send away.
me: Verb, Aorist, Middle, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Present, Middle, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means to leave or to say goodbye. It describes the act of departing from a person or place, with attention to taking one’s leave rather than remaining. The central idea is separation through departure. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, appearing in Mark, Luke, Acts, and 2 Corinthians. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its normal meaning remains straightforward: to leave or to say good-bye.

“For” is a connecting word that introduces a reason, explanation, or supporting thought. It links what follows with what has just been said, helping the reader see why a statement is made or how the next thought relates to it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 1,041 times, so it serves this linking function widely rather than naming a person, object, or action. Its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central role is to connect an explanation or reason to the preceding words.

d: On the right hand, right hand, right.

e.t: This word means “right” or “the right side,” referring to the side opposite the left. It can identify a location, direction, or position, and it may describe someone or something situated on that side. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 54 times, showing regular use for physical placement and related positional descriptions. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains the right side or a position associated with it.

d: A calculation, reasoning, thought, movement of thought, deliberation, plotting.

e.t: This word means “reasoning” or “thought”—the mental activity of considering, weighing, or forming ideas. It can describe thoughts within a person or reasoning expressed in discussion. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, showing a recurring focus on what people think and reason about. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: The roof (of a house), the top of the house.

e.t: This word refers to the roof or housetop of a building—the upper, often accessible area of a house. It is used for a physical place from which someone might speak, observe events, leave quickly, or be reached by others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, including references in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts. Its basic meaning remains concrete: the top or roof of a house, rather than a figurative idea by itself.

me: Verb, Aorist, Passive, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word means “to be broken off” or “to break off,” describing something severed from what it was attached to. In its three occurrences in the Greek New Testament, it appears in Romans 11:17, 19, and 20. The expression is used for branches being cut away or removed, so its basic sense is separation through breaking rather than merely moving or leaving. The precise force in each sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains being broken off from a former connection.

This word means “afraid,” describing someone who is experiencing fear or alarm. It is used in the Greek New Testament five times, referring to people portrayed as fearful in different situations. The central idea remains the inward response of fear, while the surrounding passage determines what caused that fear and how strongly it was felt. Its occurrences are found in Luke, Acts, and Revelation, showing that the word can describe fear in both ordinary encounters and extraordinary events.

d: To remind, possibly: to remind again.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means to remind someone, or to remind them again of something already known. It describes bringing a matter back to a person’s attention rather than introducing it as entirely new. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its basic meaning is clear even though this single occurrence gives limited opportunity to observe its wider use. It focuses on the act of recalling something to mind.

d: On whom a curse has been invoked, accursed, doomed to destruction.

e.t: “Cursed” describes someone or something placed under a curse. It is a concise word of adverse designation: the person or thing is not being described as favored, honored, or approved, but as standing under a curse. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs only twice, both in Galatians 3:10 and 3:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force there.

d: To shine upon, give light to.
me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to shine on,” describing light appearing or being directed upon something. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 5:14. Its basic sense concerns the arrival or giving of light; the surrounding verse determines the precise force of that action in context.

d: A creeping creature, reptile, especially a serpent.

e.t: This word refers to reptiles—animals that crawl or move close to the ground. It is a plural noun, so it describes more than one such creature rather than a single animal. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times: twice in Acts, once in Romans, and once in James. These references place it among broad lists or descriptions of creatures, but the precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: reptiles or crawling animals.

d: (a) to be jealous, (b) to be jealous of, with acc. of a person; to be eager for, to be eager to possess, with acc. of a thing.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “be eager” or “to desire.” It describes an active longing or strong wish for something, functioning as an action word rather than naming a person or object. Its sense can be understood broadly as wanting or earnestly seeking, while the surrounding verse determines what is desired and whether that desire is commendable or harmful. It occurs 11 times in the Greek New Testament, including several passages in 1 Corinthians. [p03:word:greek-nt:G2206:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G2206:occurrences]

Terah is a personal name, referring to a man named in the genealogy recorded in Luke 3:34. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once and functions as a proper name rather than as a general description, action, or quality. Its meaning is therefore primarily identification: it points to the individual called Terah. The surrounding genealogy supplies the specific family setting for the name’s use.

d: Beautiful, as an outward sign of the inward good, noble, honorable character; good, worthy, honorable, noble, and seen to be so.

e.t: This word means “good” and describes something as beneficial, valuable, fitting, or worthy of approval. It expresses a positive quality rather than merely identifying something as present or acceptable. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 101 times, showing broad use for people, things, actions, and outcomes that are regarded positively. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and subject being described.

e.t: This word means “to follow”—to go after someone or remain behind them as they move. It describes the act of following rather than a separate person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, both rendered with the idea of following. Its ordinary meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines whom someone follows and why. The word appears once in Luke and once in Acts, showing the same basic action across both passages.

This word refers to a herald or preacher—a person who publicly announces a message. It describes someone serving as a messenger who declares what has been entrusted to him, rather than quietly keeping the message private. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, and each occurrence is rendered “preacher.” Its references span 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and 2 Peter, showing that the term is used for a recognized public messenger who proclaims God’s message.

d: To prevent, debar, hinder; from doing so and so.

e.t: This word means to prevent or hinder—to stop someone or something from moving forward, taking action, or reaching a goal. It can describe an effort that blocks another person, activity, or opportunity. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 23 times, so it is used for this general idea in several settings rather than for only one particular situation. The surrounding words determine exactly what is being blocked, but the central sense remains preventing, hindering, or stopping something from happening.

This word means “lampstand,” the stand or support on which a lamp is placed. It refers to a physical furnishing used to hold a lamp so its light can be seen, rather than being hidden. In the New Testament, it occurs 12 times across 11 verses, including passages that mention lampstands in ordinary illustrations and in sacred or heavenly settings. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a support for a lamp and its visible light.

d: Large, great, in the widest sense.
me: Adjective, Dative, Plural, Feminine, NUmerical Indiclinable (A)

e.t: This word describes something great, greater, older, or very great. It can indicate size, importance, intensity, age, or superiority, depending on what it describes in a sentence. Thus, it may refer to something impressive, something of greater degree, or someone considered greater than another. It is a widely used adjective in the Greek New Testament, occurring 243 times. Its exact force in any verse comes from the noun or person it qualifies and the surrounding context, but its central idea is marked greatness or a higher degree.

This word means “rather,” marking a preference, correction, or stronger alternative in a statement. It helps shift attention from one possibility to another, often giving the second point greater emphasis. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Luke, Romans, and Philippians. Its exact force—whether contrast, correction, or emphasis—depends on the sentence in which it appears, but its central sense is to point to what should be preferred or considered more fitting.

d: A captain (master) of a ship, ship-owner.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word refers to a ship’s “captain” or “ship owner”—the person responsible for the vessel. It is a specific term rather than a broad word for any sailor or passenger. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:11, so its normal meaning is clear, while the precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

me: Verb, Present, Active, iMperative, second, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means to be childlike or to be a child. It describes a person’s condition or manner rather than naming a specific object. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 14:20. Its basic sense is clear, while the surrounding verse and passage determine exactly how that childlike quality is being addressed there.

This word means a homeland or hometown—the place a person regards as home. It can describe the local community or country connected with someone’s origins and familiar life. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, referring to a place rather than to a person or an action. Its central idea remains the same whether the setting is a small hometown or a broader fatherland.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to flash around” or “to shine,” describing light that suddenly appears or spreads around someone or something. It functions as a verb, expressing an action rather than naming the light itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts, in references to the same kind of sudden surrounding brightness. The word’s central idea is vivid light appearing around a person or object; the surrounding passage determines the particular force of that brightness in each verse.

This word means “bad” or “evil,” describing what is morally wrong or opposed to what is good. Its central sense is negative: it identifies evil as a quality, condition, or force rather than something worthy of approval. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 78 times, so it is used broadly across different passages. The precise shade of meaning—whether referring to an evil person, action, condition, or influence—comes from the sentence and surrounding passage.

This word means “sprinkling,” referring to the act or result of sprinkling something. In the Greek New Testament, it appears two times, in Hebrews 12:24 and 1 Peter 1:2. Its wording connects with the scriptural practice of applying blood by sprinkling, but the precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. As a noun, it names an act or its result rather than describing a person or action by itself. The word therefore points to sprinkling as a significant ritual or symbolic application.

This word describes a quality of dignity and holiness—conduct marked by seriousness, honor, and moral purity. It points to a worthy character rather than mere outward respect or social status. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in 1 Timothy and Titus, where such dignity is connected with how believers and their households should be regarded and lived out. The surrounding verse explains its precise emphasis in each occurrence.

“Iron” refers to the strong metal used as a material or valuable commodity. As a noun, the word names the substance itself rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 18:12. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the metal iron. The English rendering consistently reflects this sense.

This word means “form,” referring to the recognizable shape or outward manner in which something is presented. It describes how something appears or is expressed rather than naming its inner nature by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Corinthians 7:31 and Philippians 2:7. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central sense remains the form or presentation of something.

d: Tiberias, a town in Galilee on the western border of the sea called after it.

e.t: Tiberias is the name rendered “Tiberias.” It is not a general action, quality, or spiritual concept, but a specific name used in the Greek New Testament. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, and all three occurrences are in John: 6:1, 6:23, and 21:1. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s precise role in each passage must be understood from its immediate context.

The word means a he-goat, that is, a male goat. It names the animal itself rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Hebrews 9–10. The word therefore keeps a concrete, ordinary meaning: a male goat being discussed in the passage. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding context.

d: Literal: to raise beyond, uplift; to lift oneself up, exalt oneself, to be arrogant.
me: Verb, Present, Middle, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Present, Passive, Subjunctive, first, Singular

e.t: This word describes becoming proud or lifted up in one’s own estimation—being haughty or conceited. It points to an attitude of self-exaltation rather than simple confidence: a person places himself above others or assumes an elevated position. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times in two verses, so it is uncommon but carries a clear moral sense wherever it appears. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding context.

d: To put under, lay down, suggest to, put in mind.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Present, Middle, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word expresses either putting something at risk or teaching, depending on how it functions in the sentence. Its recorded meanings include “risked,” “to risk,” “to risk/teach,” and “to teach.” It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 16:4 and 1 Timothy 4:6. Because the available wording supports both risking and teaching, the surrounding verse is needed to identify which sense is intended in a particular passage.

d: Brotherly love, love of Christian brethren.

e.t: This word means “brotherly love,” describing warm, devoted affection expressed among fellow believers. It points to love that treats others with the care and loyalty associated with close family. In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times, including teaching in Romans, 1 Thessalonians, Hebrews, 1 Peter, and 2 Peter. Its repeated use shows a consistent emphasis on sincere love within the community of God’s people.

d: A lie, falsehood, untruth; false religion.

e.t: This word means “a lie”—a falsehood rather than what is true. In the Greek New Testament, it refers to false statements or claims and is presented as the opposite of truth. It occurs 10 times across 10 verses, showing that the term is used repeatedly for falsehood in different passages. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains a lie or falsehood.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “jump up.” It describes a sudden upward movement and functions as an action word, presenting someone as rising or springing upward. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 10:50. That single occurrence supports a focused meaning rather than a broad range of uses: the word points to the act of jumping up itself. The surrounding verse determines who performs the action and why, but the word’s basic sense remains a physical upward movement.
